indicators.note: after places the word it behind the turned month
returned means the month's short form is read backwards

parts.note: FEB is the short form of February, a month

explanation.surface: Someone tailoring a suit comes back to it a month later.
explanation.definitionFit: To suit is to be appropriate for, which is the verb's sense of being proper.

clue.text: Railways admit breaking promise in way of working

indicators.note: in places the other pieces within the railways abbreviation

parts.note: BR is British Rail, the old national railways

indicators.note: breaking means the letters of the admitting word are broken up and reordered

parts.note: to have someone in is to admit them
an IOU is a written promise to pay

explanation.surface: A rail company concedes it went back on its word about working practice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking' rearranges HAVE to EHAV; that and IOU go 'in' BR.
explanation.definitionFit: Behaviour is how a person or machine acts, its conduct or manner of functioning.

indicators.note: out means a letter is taken out of the phrase for assaulted

parts.note: fell on means attacked, assaulted
one L, the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A criminal attacked someone who had been excluded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' removes one L from FELL ON.
explanation.definitionFit: A felon is someone convicted of a serious crime, a lawbreaker.

indicators.note: various means the letters come in different arrangements

explanation.surface: A gardener lists assorted plants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'various' rearranges LISTS THE.
explanation.definitionFit: Thistles are prickly wild flowering weeds, the emblem of Scotland.

parts.note: flat means plain, level ground
news that broke was revealed

explanation.surface: A rocky plain comes into view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stony' here is the slang 'stony-broke', having no money at all, not rocky.
explanation.definitionFit: Stony, short for stony-broke, is British slang for penniless.

indicators.note: up, in a down entry, means the game's name is read from bottom to top

parts.note: golf is the game; the possessive 's is just a link

explanation.surface: Sell up once the game is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the game's up' is the idiom for being found out; here 'up' turns GOLF upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Flog is British slang for selling something, often cheaply or hard.

parts.note: the answer to 29 across is a Scottish pet name; its full form with a possessive s is also a herb once eaten in salads

explanation.surface: Entry 29's choice of salad greens.
explanation.walkthrough: SANDY is short for the Scots name whose possessive is spelt like the old pot-herb, eaten in salads like celery.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexanders is an umbelliferous herb formerly grown as a vegetable and used in salads.

clue.text: Promise to bring silver up from the cellar

parts.note: to bode is to promise or portend

indicators.note: up, in a down entry, means the silver symbol is read upwards

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: Someone vows to fetch the silverware from the basement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns AG to GA under BODE.
explanation.definitionFit: A bodega is a Spanish wine shop or wine store, originally a cellar.

clue.text: Forced or drove A.B. off ship

indicators.note: forced means these letters are wrenched into a new order

explanation.surface: A sailor was forced or driven off the vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forced' rearranges OR DROVE AB.
explanation.definitionFit: Going over the side of a vessel into the water means leaving it.

indicators.note: intruding in means the letter for one is pushed inside the surname

parts.note: Jane Eyre, Charlotte Bronte's heroine
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone breaks into Jane's home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'intruding in' puts I inside EYRE.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyrie is an eagle's nest built high on a crag.

clue.text: Everything, they say, combined to create this master stroke

indicators.note: they say signals that the word for everything is heard rather than written

parts.note: whole means everything
in one means combined, united

explanation.surface: Everything came together to produce a brilliant shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'they say' turns WHOLE into its sound-alike HOLE; 'master stroke' is a golfing sense, a single shot from tee to cup.
explanation.definitionFit: A golfer's ace from the tee is the supreme single shot of the game.

parts.note: DR is the abbreviation for doctor, a medical man
to lend an ear is to pay attention

explanation.surface: A depressing doctor wins someone's ear.
explanation.definitionFit: Drear is a poetic form of dreary, meaning dismal and dull.

clue.text: Conceit'- against it in' any case

parts.note: V is short for versus, against

indicators.note: in places the word it inside the word any
case means the word any forms a case around the other piece

explanation.surface: A warning against conceit, whatever happens.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'in any case' as 'anyway', an aside; the solver must split it into a container instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Conceit is excessive pride in oneself, the same as self-admiring pride.

clue.text: Yellowish-brown rock the French used to make concrete

parts.note: tan is a yellowish-brown colour
Gib is a short name for the Rock of Gibraltar
le is French for the

explanation.surface: Builders mix brown stone with a French recipe to make concrete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'concrete' looks like the building material, but it is the adjective for something real and solid.
explanation.definitionFit: Concrete as an adjective means real and touchable, perceptible by the senses.

clue.text: Agree with nothing, and lose heart

parts.note: to fall in with means to agree with
love is nothing, nil, in tennis

explanation.surface: Agree to nothing and become discouraged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lose heart' looks like despair, but losing one's heart to someone is the romantic sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose one's heart to someone is an idiom for becoming smitten with them.

explanation.surface: Happy-birthday messages are probable.
explanation.definitionFit: Birthday wishes are written on greeting cards; the idiom for probable means expected to happen.

clue.text: Spare no effort reconstructing East Pakistan

indicators.note: reconstructing means the letters are put together again in a different order

explanation.surface: Rebuilding the former East Pakistan takes great effort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reconstructing' rearranges E with PAKISTAN; East Pakistan became Bangladesh.
explanation.definitionFit: To take pains is an idiom for trying very hard, being careful and thorough.

indicators.note: deprived of means a letter is taken away from the song

parts.note: a psalm is a sacred song

explanation.surface: A singer misses out on the runner-up award.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deprived of' removes S from PSALM.
explanation.definitionFit: The palm branch was a victor's emblem, so it stands for the winning honour.

clue.text: Cash note now, losing nothing — it's time to sell

parts.note: the mark was German currency, cash
E is a musical note

indicators.note: losing means a letter drops out of the word for now

parts.note: today means now, nowadays
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Cash notes are now worthless: it's time to sell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing' removes O from TODAY to give TDAY.
explanation.definitionFit: A town's weekly trading day is when stallholders bring goods to sell.

indicators.note: raised, in a down entry, means the matter word is read upwards

parts.note: pus is matter discharged from a wound
the press is journalists collectively

explanation.surface: Journalists raise a matter that someone wants hushed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns PUS to SUP; 'matter' looks like a topic, not pus.
explanation.definitionFit: To suppress information is to conceal it, keep it from coming out.

explanation.surface: Tending to become a rogue.
explanation.definitionFit: A stage's slope is its inclination; a dissolute pleasure-seeking man is a rakehell.

clue.text: An old ruler, represented as a versatile person

indicators.note: represented means the letters of these words are presented again in a new order

explanation.surface: A former monarch is depicted as a person of many talents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'represented' rearranges AN OLD RULER.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricketer good at batting and bowling is the classic example of a multi-skilled player.

parts.note: art means pictures, paintings
Ben-Hur is the famous film and novel

explanation.surface: Paintings show Ben as a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ben' asks for the second half of BEN-HUR.
explanation.definitionFit: King Arthur is the legendary British ruler of Camelot.

clue.text: Like a hare in shelter, gazin' intently

indicators.note: in places the gazing word inside the shelter word

parts.note: lee is the sheltered side, shelter from wind
poring means gazing intently; the dropped g in gazin' says drop it here too

explanation.surface: A hare sits in cover, staring hard.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'gazin'' is the hint: PORING loses its G to become PORIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Leporine is the adjective from Latin lepus, describing anything resembling the long-eared animal.

clue.text: He's landed, having put down around start of runway

indicators.note: around means the first word goes round the letter

parts.note: laid means put down

indicators.note: start of means take only the first letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A pilot touched down around the beginning of the runway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He's landed' sounds like a pilot; it means a landowner. 'around' puts R inside LAID.
explanation.definitionFit: A laird is a Scottish landowner, one of the landed gentry.

parts.note: to spar is to scrap, to fight, so scraps are spars

indicators.note: end in means take the last letter of the following word

explanation.surface: Thin rations of leftovers mark the close of a famine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scraps' looks like leftover food; it is the verb, fights.
explanation.definitionFit: Sparse means thinly scattered, scanty, which is the sense of meagre.

clue.text: Obtain control, by the sound of it

annotationWithheld.clue: Obtain control, by the sound of it

explanation.surface: Direction on the left.
explanation.definitionFit: Port means deportment, how one carries oneself; on a ship it is the left side.

clue.text: Country's. part in affair is honourable

indicators.note: part in means a run of letters sits within the following words

explanation.surface: A nation's role in a matter is creditable.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means of Ireland, so it stands for that nation's possessive.

clue.text: Agreed to love enemy who's accepted new opinion

parts.note: love is nil in tennis, the letter O

indicators.note: who's accepted means the enemy word takes another letter inside it

parts.note: a foe is an enemy
mind means opinion, as in 'to my mind'

explanation.surface: Someone agreed to love an enemy after taking on a fresh viewpoint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'who's accepted' puts N inside FOE.
explanation.definitionFit: Of one mind is an idiom for being unanimous, in full accord.

indicators.note: out means the letters are put out of their order and rearranged

explanation.surface: A creased garment has been pressed flat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges IT'S IRONED.
explanation.definitionFit: To upset someone is to confuse or unsettle them, to make them lose their bearings.

explanation.surface: A plucky Scotsman.
explanation.definitionFit: A common Scottish pet name for Alexander; full of grains of sand, gritty.
